questions.q: Why does the recommended story structure start with the inherited state rather than jumping straight to the fixes?
options: Because a plainly described 'before' is what makes the 'after' numbers meaningful — improvement only reads as improvement in contrast to a clear starting point
Because interviewers only care about problems, not solutions
Because it takes longer to describe the fixes, so the inherited state is used as a time filler
Because SQL Server documentation requires listing problems before solutions
questions.explain: Without a concrete before state, an after state has nothing to be compared against. Describing MERSQL01's actual condition first is what makes '15-minute RPO' or '12-minute resolution' land as real improvements.

questions.q: The lesson says interviewers want the 'mechanism' when you describe the production incident. What does that mean in this capstone's context?
options: Explaining specifically which DMVs you queried, what they showed, and what action you took — not just stating that the issue got fixed
Explaining the internal mechanics of how SQL Server's storage engine writes pages to disk
Providing the exact server hardware specifications
Listing every table in DispatchDB affected by the incident
questions.explain: The mechanism is the specific technical path from symptom to resolution — sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_exec_sessions, sys.dm_tran_locks, then KILL 82 — which demonstrates real diagnostic skill rather than a vague outcome claim.

questions.q: Why does the change management deployment (Lesson 68) belong in this story at all, given that the incident (Lesson 67) already demonstrates problem-solving skill?
options: It proves the improvements are durable and repeatable — a process change, not just a one-time fix — which a single resolved incident doesn't demonstrate by itself
It doesn't really belong; the story would be equally strong without it
It's included only because it happened chronologically after the incident
It replaces the need to mention the incident at all
questions.explain: The incident shows crisis response; the safe deployment shows that a repeatable, disciplined process is now in place going forward — together they show both reactive and proactive competence.

questions.q: Which of these is the most effective way to state the RPO improvement, per this lesson's emphasis on specific numbers?
options: "RPO went from undefined — potentially weeks of data loss — to 15 minutes, once scheduled log backups were in place"
"I made backups better"
"The database is now backed up regularly, which is good practice"
"Backups happen more often than they used to"
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts vague claims ('I improved things') with specific before/after numbers. Naming the actual RPO shift from undefined to 15 minutes is the concrete version that lands.

questions.q: The lesson lists a follow-up question an interviewer might ask: 'What would you have done if killing session 82 hadn't resolved it?' What is this question really testing?
options: Whether you understand the incident as a methodology you can adapt, rather than a single memorized script that only works for that exact scenario
Whether you remember the exact session ID number
Whether KILL is a valid T-SQL command
Whether DispatchDB was in the FULL recovery model
questions.explain: Follow-up questions like this probe whether you truly understand the triage methodology (check further, escalate, consider a service restart, etc.) rather than having just memorized what happened to work in one specific case.
